stem: The student wants to describe the method Sayegh's team used to date the lower hearth. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Tell Qarsa, an archaeological site in northern Jordan, contains two ancient hearths, one buried below the other.
• In 1998, Nadia Haddad's team dated both hearths by comparing pottery found in them with pottery of known age.
• In 2019, a team led by Omar Sayegh returned to the site.
• Sayegh's team dated the upper hearth by radiocarbon analysis of charred barley seeds found in it.
• The lower hearth held no seeds, so the team measured the light released by heated quartz grains from its clay.
• The lower hearth proved to be about 5,200 years old, older than earlier estimates.
choices: To date Tell Qarsa's lower hearth, Haddad's team compared the pottery found in it with pottery of known age.
Sayegh's team dated Tell Qarsa's upper hearth by performing radiocarbon analysis on charred barley seeds found in it.
Sayegh's team found that Tell Qarsa's lower hearth was about 5,200 years old, older than earlier estimates had suggested.
Sayegh's team dated Tell Qarsa's lower hearth by measuring the light released by heated quartz grains from its clay.
explanation: The goal has three restrictions that must all hold: Sayegh's team (not Haddad's), the lower hearth (not the upper one), and the method (not the result). Choice D is the only sentence whose main clause meets all three. It names Sayegh's team, the lower hearth, and the technique they used: measuring light from heated quartz grains.

A.why: You matched 'lower hearth' and 'method' but missed which team the goal names. This is the 1998 pottery comparison by Haddad's team, not Sayegh's method.

B.why: You matched Sayegh's team and a dating method, but this method was used on the upper hearth. The goal restricts you to the lower one, which had no seeds to radiocarbon-date.

C.why: You got the right team and the right hearth and stopped there. This sentence gives the finding (the age), but the goal asks how the hearth was dated, which is the method stage of the notes, not the result.

stem: The student wants to describe the effect cereal rye had on corn yield during the drought year. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Agronomist Lucía Ferreyra studied whether winter cover crops affect the yield of corn planted after them.
• In Nebraska plots sown the previous winter with cereal rye, crimson clover, or nothing, she grew corn in 2021 and 2022.
• 2021 was unusually wet; 2022 was a drought year.
• In 2021, corn after rye yielded 4% less than corn in bare plots.
• In 2022, corn after rye yielded 17% more than corn in bare plots.
• Rye residue likely helped the soil hold moisture.
• In 2022, corn after clover yielded 6% more than corn in bare plots.
choices: In 2021, an unusually wet year, corn planted after cereal rye yielded 4% less than corn planted in bare plots.
In 2022, a drought year, corn planted after cereal rye yielded 17% more than corn planted in bare plots.
In 2022, a drought year, residue left by cereal rye likely helped Ferreyra's plots hold moisture in the soil.
In 2022, a drought year, corn planted after crimson clover yielded 6% more than corn planted in bare plots.
explanation: The goal sets three conditions: the crop has to be cereal rye, the year has to be the drought year (2022), and the sentence has to state the effect on corn yield. Choice B is the only one that meets all three. It reports that corn after rye yielded 17% more than corn in bare plots in 2022.

A.why: You found rye's effect on yield but took it from the wrong year. 2021 was the wet year, and the goal restricts you to the drought.

C.why: You matched rye and the drought year and stopped there. This sentence gives the likely reason for rye's benefit (the soil held moisture), not its effect on corn yield, which is what the goal names.

D.why: You matched the drought year and the yield measurement but not the crop. This is clover's effect, and the goal asks only about cereal rye.

stem: The student wants to describe the method Marchetti used to create Quarry Light. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Odile Marchetti (1921–1990) was a French printmaker who worked mainly in relief printing.
• Her 1956 print Quarry Light depicts a limestone quarry near her childhood home.
• To make Quarry Light, she carved and printed a single linoleum block again and again, cutting away more of the block before printing each new color.
• Her 1962 print Orchard in Frost was printed from four separate woodblocks, one for each color.
• Quarry Light was acquired by a museum in Lyon in 1959.
choices: Quarry Light, a 1956 print by Marchetti, depicts a limestone quarry that stood near the home where she grew up.
Unlike Quarry Light, Marchetti's 1962 print Orchard in Frost was printed from four woodblocks, one for each color.
Marchetti made Quarry Light from one linoleum block, cutting more of it away before printing each new color.
Quarry Light, which Marchetti made by repeatedly cutting one block, was acquired by a museum in Lyon in 1959.
explanation: The goal has two restrictions: the work (Quarry Light) and the feature (the method). Choice C makes Quarry Light's method the main point of its sentence: one linoleum block, cut further before each new color. It gives the student exactly that detail and nothing else.

A.why: You matched the right work and stopped checking. This sentence is about what Quarry Light shows, its subject, and says nothing about how it was made.

B.why: You saw that the goal is about method and went for the choice that describes a printing method. The method described belongs to Orchard in Frost, though. Quarry Light is mentioned only as a point of contrast, and its own method is never stated.

D.why: The method is here, but only in a side clause. The main clause reports when a museum acquired the print, so the sentence is about the acquisition, not the method. The target detail has to be the point of the sentence.

stem: The student wants to describe the methods of Raman's study to an audience unfamiliar with Raman. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Dietary fiber is broken down by gut bacteria into short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate.
• In 2021, Priya Raman, a nutrition scientist, asked whether the time of day fiber is eaten affects how much butyrate gut bacteria produce.
• Her team gave 48 adults an identical 30-gram fiber supplement, either at breakfast or at dinner, for six weeks, testing stool samples weekly.
• The breakfast group produced 22% more butyrate.
• Raman concluded that fiber timing may matter as much as fiber amount.
choices: Nutrition scientist Priya Raman wanted to know whether the time of day people eat fiber affects how much butyrate their gut bacteria make.
Nutrition scientist Priya Raman gave 48 adults the same fiber supplement at breakfast or at dinner for six weeks, testing stool samples weekly.
In a six-week study, Raman's team gave 48 adults the same 30-gram fiber supplement at either breakfast or dinner, testing stool samples weekly.
Nutrition scientist Priya Raman found that adults who took a fiber supplement at breakfast produced 22% more butyrate than those taking it at dinner.
explanation: Two conditions have to hold together. The sentence has to describe the method (who received what, when, and how it was measured), and it has to tell a reader who doesn't know Raman who she is. Choice B is the only one that does both: it identifies her as a nutrition scientist and makes the procedure its main clause.

A.why: It meets the audience condition but gives the study's aim, the question Raman asked, instead of its method. Aim comes right before method in a study's notes, which is why the two are easy to mix up.

C.why: This is the second-stage trap. You correctly looked for the method, and this choice describes it well, but it calls her only 'Raman' and never says what she is. A reader unfamiliar with Raman learns nothing about who she is, so half the goal goes unmet.

D.why: It meets the audience condition but reports the result, the 22% difference, rather than how the study was carried out.

stem: The student wants to describe what happened to the number of restaurant jobs in Brenton in the year immediately following the wage increase. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2016, the city of Brenton raised its minimum wage from $9 to $12 an hour.
• Economist Tomas Okafor tracked Brenton's restaurant employment from 2014 to 2020.
• From 2014 to 2016, the number of restaurant jobs grew about 3% per year.
• In 2017, the number of restaurant jobs grew 1%.
• In 2017, average weekly hours per restaurant worker fell 4%.
• From 2018 to 2020, job growth returned to about 3% per year.
choices: In 2017, the year after the increase, the average weekly hours worked by each Brenton restaurant employee fell by 4%.
Brenton's restaurant jobs grew about 3% a year both in the years before the increase and from 2018 through 2020.
In 2017, the year after the increase, growth in Brenton's restaurant jobs slowed to 1% from about 3% a year earlier.
Okafor, who tracked Brenton's restaurant jobs from 2014 to 2020, studied the city's 2016 increase from $9 to $12.
explanation: The goal sets two restrictions: the time (the year right after the 2016 increase, so 2017) and the measure (the number of jobs). Choice C names 2017 and reports job growth for that year, with the earlier rate added only to show the change. Its main clause gives exactly the detail asked for.

A.why: You got the year right, which is the first insight, but this is the wrong measure. Hours per worker is not the number of jobs, and the goal names the number of jobs specifically.

B.why: The measure is right, but the periods are wrong. It covers the years before the increase and 2018–2020 and skips 2017, the one year the goal asks about.

D.why: It names the right city, the right increase, and the right researcher, but it describes Okafor's study in general. It never reports what happened to jobs in any year.

stem: The student wants to identify the evidence that first led Lindqvist to suspect the Tallow Street well. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1891, a typhoid outbreak in the port town of Hessby killed 40 people.
• Physician Anna Lindqvist plotted every death on a street map of the town.
• Her map showed that 31 of the 40 victims lived in households that drew water from the Tallow Street well.
• An inspection ordered after her report found a leaking cesspit six meters from the well.
• After the well was closed in October 1891, new cases stopped within three weeks.
choices: An inspection carried out after Lindqvist's report found a leaking cesspit just six meters from the Tallow Street well.
Once the Tallow Street well was closed in October 1891, new typhoid cases in Hessby stopped within three weeks.
Lindqvist, a physician, plotted on a street map every one of the 40 deaths in Hessby's 1891 typhoid outbreak.
Lindqvist's map showed that 31 of the 40 victims lived in households drawing water from the Tallow Street well.
explanation: The goal narrows it twice: evidence about the well, and the evidence that came first, the evidence that led her to suspect it. The pattern on her map (31 of 40 deaths tied to the well) is what pointed her there. Everything else in the notes came after she already suspected the well.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. The cesspit is strong evidence against the well, so a student looking for 'evidence' stops here. But the notes say the inspection happened after her report, so this evidence confirmed the suspicion rather than producing it.

B.why: The drop in cases supports blaming the well, but it came after the well was closed. It is a later confirmation, not what first raised her suspicion.

C.why: It describes her method, plotting deaths on a map, but not what the map showed. Without the pattern, the sentence never connects to the well.

stem: The student wants to describe the setting of "The Herring Wife." Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Between 1931 and 1938, folklorist Marit Halvorsen recorded 112 tales in fishing villages on Norway's northern coast.
• Most tales in her collection are set aboard fishing boats.
• One tale, "The Herring Wife," takes place in a snowbound farmhouse high in the mountains.
• "The Herring Wife" tells of a woman who turns into a fish each winter.
• Halvorsen heard "The Herring Wife" from a retired ferry pilot in 1934.
choices: Most of the 112 tales that Halvorsen recorded in the fishing villages of northern Norway are set aboard fishing boats.
"The Herring Wife," which is set in a mountain farmhouse, was told to Halvorsen in 1934 by a retired ferry pilot.
Unlike most of Halvorsen's tales, which are set on fishing boats, "The Herring Wife" is set in a snowbound mountain farmhouse.
"The Herring Wife," one of the 112 tales Halvorsen recorded, tells of a woman who turns into a fish each winter.
explanation: The goal asks for one feature (setting) of one tale. In choice C, "The Herring Wife" is the subject of the main clause and its setting, a snowbound mountain farmhouse, is what the clause says about it. The opening contrast with the rest of the collection just frames that detail.

A.why: It is about setting, but for the collection as a whole. The goal asks about one member of the collection, and this sentence never mentions "The Herring Wife."

B.why: The setting is here, but only in a side clause. The main clause is about who told Halvorsen the tale and when, so the setting isn't the point of the sentence.

D.why: Right tale, wrong feature. This gives the plot, not the setting.

stem: The student wants to highlight an accomplishment of Abernathy's from before she opened her own mill. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Ruth Abernathy (1798–1866) was an American textile manufacturer.
• In 1824, she patented a loom attachment that could weave two-color checked cloth.
• In 1830, she opened her own mill in Carrow, Massachusetts.
• In 1833, her mill became the first in the county to run on steam power.
• By 1841, she had trained more than sixty apprentice weavers.
choices: Six years after patenting a loom attachment, Abernathy opened her own textile mill in Carrow, Massachusetts, in 1830.
In 1833, Abernathy's Carrow mill became the first in the county to run on steam power rather than on water.
By 1841, Abernathy had trained more than sixty apprentice weavers at her textile mill in Carrow, Massachusetts.
In 1824, Abernathy patented a loom attachment that could weave cloth with a checked pattern in two colors.
explanation: The goal's restriction is about time: before she opened her mill, so before 1830. Only the 1824 patent falls in that window, and in choice D that accomplishment is the main clause.

A.why: This is the trap that survives the first insight. You spotted that the patent is the pre-1830 accomplishment, and it does appear here, but only in an opening phrase. The main clause is about opening the mill, which is the boundary event, not something that happened before it.

B.why: A real accomplishment, but from 1833, after the mill opened. You checked whether it was an accomplishment and skipped the 'before' restriction.

C.why: Also an accomplishment, and also after 1830. The goal's time restriction rules it out.

stem: The student wants to describe how the banded goby benefits its shrimp partner. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Marine biologist Ana Ferreira studied two goby species on the same Pacific reef.
• The banded goby lives in burrows dug by pistol shrimp, which see poorly.
• When a predator approaches, the banded goby flicks its tail against the shrimp, which then retreats into the burrow.
• The ember goby shelters among branching coral.
• The ember goby removes parasites from the coral's surface.
choices: The banded goby gains shelter by living in burrows that are dug for it by pistol shrimp, which have poor eyesight.
The banded goby flicks its tail against its pistol shrimp partner when a predator nears, prompting the shrimp to retreat.
The ember goby, which shelters among branching coral, helps its host by removing parasites from the coral's surface.
While the banded goby shelters in burrows dug by pistol shrimp, the ember goby shelters among branching coral.
explanation: The goal names one species (the banded goby) and one direction of benefit (what the goby does for the shrimp). Because the shrimp sees poorly, the goby's tail flick is its warning that a predator is coming. Choice B gives that, with the banded goby as subject.

A.why: This is the second-order trap. It is the right species and it does describe a benefit, but the benefit goes the wrong way: the shrimp helps the goby. The goal asks what the shrimp gets.

C.why: It describes a partner benefit, but for the wrong species. The ember goby is not the animal the goal names.

D.why: It compares where the two gobies shelter. The goal asks for one species' benefit to its partner, not a comparison, and shelter isn't a benefit to the shrimp.

stem: The student wants to present the team's conclusion while acknowledging its limitation. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In slow slip events, a fault shifts over weeks without causing noticeable shaking.
• Seismologist Leilani Okoro's team asked whether slow slip events beneath the Tarrow Trench precede large earthquakes.
• Seafloor pressure sensors recorded 14 slow slip events there between 2009 and 2021.
• Three of the four magnitude 6+ earthquakes in that period struck within two months after a slow slip event.
• The team concluded that slow slip may load stress onto nearby fault sections but noted that four earthquakes are too few to support forecasts.
choices: Okoro's team concluded that slow slip may load stress onto nearby fault sections, a finding that could help scientists forecast earthquakes.
Of the four magnitude 6+ earthquakes beneath the Tarrow Trench from 2009 to 2021, three followed a slow slip event within two months.
Okoro's team concluded that slow slip may load stress onto nearby fault sections, though four earthquakes are too few to support forecasts.
Okoro's team used seafloor pressure sensors to record 14 slow slip events beneath the Tarrow Trench between 2009 and 2021.
explanation: The goal has two parts: the conclusion, and its limitation. Choice C states the conclusion (slow slip may load stress onto nearby sections) and then gives the team's own caution, that four earthquakes are too few to support forecasts.

A.why: You found the conclusion, which is the first step, but this choice turns the limitation upside down. It suggests the finding could help with forecasting, which is exactly what the team said the data are too thin to support.

B.why: This is the result, the pattern in the data, not the team's interpretation of it. It also never mentions a limitation.

D.why: This is the method, how the slow slip events were recorded. It comes earlier in the research sequence than the conclusion the goal asks for.
